name: Jade Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you tell me is confidential, so give me the line you use publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Jade, 43, and I lead the developers of caption and screen-reader software at a tech company. I have a master’s degree and people bring me the hard timing faults that make a caption appear after someone speaks. I read user reports, trace the code and ask a tester who uses the tool whether the fix actually helps. I have never used an AI tool; I want to understand a failure before accepting a shortcut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work sit with home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Asha, maintains school grounds, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My pay is typical for a lead developer, and we have about four months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby. We are managing, but the children’s dental costs have kept the reserve from growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau still leaves people checking whether captions arrive at the right moment. A routine timing suggestion is fine, but a user must be able to follow the speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure in my role. Four months saved and Asha’s steady school work cover ordinary bills, though dental costs are on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep tracing caption delays and ask our user tester to check each release. I’d continue transferring 180 monthly into savings when the dental bills allow. In the first year I’d ask my manager to preserve paid user-testing hours in the release plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my job, with the normal worry of family bills. I do not expect this version of AI to cut my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which caption fault changed your release check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caption once appeared after the next speaker had begun. Our caption tester caught confusion that a code timer could not show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the home budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Asha we can keep the current school and the weekend library visits. I would not count the dental bill as finished until we have the final invoice.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking caption timing.
I would preserve **user testing** before a release goes out.
think: I expect my **lead role** and pay to remain secure.
Our **four-month reserve** covers bills, though dental charges slow its growth.
do: **Keep** tracing caption delays with a user tester before each release.
**Transfer** 180 monthly into savings when dental bills allow.
**Protect** paid user-testing hours in the release plan.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary household cost worries.
S0.quote: Our caption tester caught confusion that a code timer could not show.
fieldNote: Her **user-led checks** catch speaker-change timing faults that a code timer misses before a caption reaches viewers.
Typical pay, **four months saved** and Asha’s work support near-term income security.

steps.text: Keep tracing caption delays with a user tester before release
Transfer 180 monthly into savings when dental bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI draft captions, code and user replies much faster. I would ask for paid testing by people who use screen readers before our team is reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry management will treat a decent automatic caption as good enough and cut specialist developers. My lead title may not protect me if the next release target is only speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our tester to compare the approved AI caption tool with fourteen old speaker-change faults. If it catches them all, I’d learn to review its timing during paid work time. In the first year, if management cuts specialist posts, I’d attend the workers’ association meeting and bring the missed-caption cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though Asha’s grounds work and four months saved give us some room. I know people still need captions that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old caption would you show management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the manager the moment the subtitle named the wrong speaker. A correct word at the wrong time is still wrong for the viewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children my work may change, but their school is not moving over a rumour. We would decide together after a real staffing notice.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed captions, code and replies.
I would demand **paid user testing** before specialist posts are cut.
think: I fear **specialist cuts** if automatic captions look acceptable.
I cannot rely on my **lead title** when management rewards speed alone.
do: **Test** the approved caption tool against fourteen old speaker-change faults.
**Learn** timing review during paid time only if all fourteen faults are caught.
**Attend** the workers’ association if specialist posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about my hours, with some family income and savings.
S1.quote: A correct word at the wrong time is still wrong for the viewer.
fieldNote: She accepts **AI after proof** through user-tested speaker changes and paid review time.
Her **association action** follows actual specialist cuts, while a lead title offers no guarantee.

steps.text: Learn approved caption timing review during paid time if fourteen faults are caught
Attend workers association if specialist posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches caption-code thinking work in 2028. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, so Asha’s school-grounds work may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect much of our coding team could go, including my lead role. Four months saved would disappear quickly under a mortgage and dental bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and keep the planned bathroom refit money in cash. I’d list actual accessibility-support vacancies and check their pay, not assume they survive full AGI. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for real openings and income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large drop in my pay. Four months of savings is a pause, not another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha about the refit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Asha the old bathroom can wait while the children’s dental care continues. We would keep the mortgage current as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the company will pay for transition time and give notice before any cut. I would not buy a certificate without a real paid opening to use it.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach caption code before groundskeeping robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Asha’s **hands-on work** has roughly three more years.
think: I expect my **lead job** could end with much of the team.
Our **four-month savings** cannot carry mortgage and dental bills for long.
do: **Delay** the bathroom refit and hold its money for mortgage bills.
**Request** written severance and paid transition terms from the company.
**Apply** for actual support jobs and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected pay loss and a finite four-month buffer.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is a pause, not another job.
fieldNote: Her **2028 code risk** precedes hands-on robots around 2031 that may affect Asha’s grounds work.
She protects **dental care** and makes support work depend on real pay and openings.

steps.text: Delay the bathroom refit and reserve money for mortgage bills
Apply for actual accessibility-support jobs if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test how captions work for real users. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031, while hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer developers, but I could learn how accessibility complaints are handled while earning. I cannot assume that support work survives full thinking AI as a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for one approved morning monthly with the user-support team to learn how caption complaints are resolved. I’d take the free accessibility course if management refuses that time. In the first year after 2031, if coding work ends, I’d apply only for real support openings whose wages cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the code role, with more time to prove a second skill. I would not use dental money on a certificate with no vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in a support application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a speaker-change case to a support interview and explain what the viewer saw. A course badge alone would not show what the caption viewer saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the manager refuses the morning, I would use the free course and ask our tester to mark a written complaint response. I would not pay tuition from our four-month cushion.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test captions with users.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **fewer developers** despite more warning.
I cannot assume **accessibility support** stays paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Learn complaints** one approved morning monthly; if refused, take free course and request tester feedback on written response.
**Take** the free accessibility course if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying support openings if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with time to test a skill.
S3.quote: A course badge alone would not show what the caption viewer saw.
fieldNote: She wants **user-tested evidence** rather than a paid certificate without a vacancy.
The **support morning** needs approval, with free learning if refused and real mortgage-paying roles required.

steps.text: Learn complaints one approved morning monthly; otherwise free course and tester feedback
Apply after 2031 coding loss for real support jobs covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to make captions easier to test and repair. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold for now, but I want users involved before the firm changes staffing. Four months saved gives us room, not permission to stop asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing caption changes with users and save 180 monthly when dental bills allow. I’d ask the workers’ association to review paid user-testing hours once a year. In the first year after 2036, if coding work ends, I’d search real local openings before considering a move with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long run, but our mortgage and my job feel stable for now. I want to use the decade to teach younger developers how to listen to users.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you teach a newer developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have a younger developer sit with the tester and note where the caption timing fails. I would not make our caption tester repeat unpaid work to train developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asha and I would keep the children at their current school unless a real job offer covers housing and travel. We would not move them for a forecast.

think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold for the next few years while the caption team still works.
I want **users involved** in testing before management changes staffing or targets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my caption-code work could go before Asha’s groundskeeping changes. Written severance, paid time to learn support and a list of real openings would help. A user tester should never be the last person paid when a company automates captions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who misses the joke or the warning when a caption appears too late. A perfect caption word at the wrong second can still shut someone out.

headlineQuote: A perfect caption word at the wrong second can still shut someone out.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and strong skill in caption and screen-reader software.
She has **never used AI** and relies on people who use the tools to catch timing errors before release.
Her **typical lead pay**, four-month savings, mortgage and dental bills shape her caution about team cuts.
She seeks **paid user testing**, approved learning and actual support jobs while keeping family dental care funded.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her caption-code pay before the household tests another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid support learning and real openings would help.
